chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Amr ibn Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Udhafir, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man brings sheep from the mountain, and among them is a hired Zoroastrian and a Christian. If a rash (or sudden illness/condition) befalls them, he brings them to him salted. He said: 'He should not eat them.'

I said: If it is during the time of an obligatory prayer, and the ground does not allow him to stand or prostrate on it due to the abundance of snow, water, rain, and mud, is it permissible for him to perform the obligatory prayer while seated in a litter (or mount)?
He said: 'Yes, it is like the ship. If he can stand, he stands; otherwise, he sits. And in all such cases, God is more deserving of excuse.'
God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'But man is a witness against himself.'

key_terms.اللَّهُ أَوْلَى بِالْعُذْرِ: God is more deserving of excuse/leniency
key_terms.الْعَارِضَةُ: A sudden condition or rash, often referring to illness or a physical impediment
key_terms.الْمَحْمِلُ: A litter, seat, or mount used for carrying someone
key_terms.بِمَنْزِلَةِ السَّفِينَةِ: Like the ship (a legal analogy for prayer posture)

ai.seo_question: How should one perform obligatory prayers when the ground is covered in deep snow or mud making standing impossible?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of *al-'udhr* (excuse) in prayer, ruling that difficult terrain conditions justify praying seated, analogous to the concession granted for travelers on ships. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on practical ease (*taysir*) when physical constraints, such as deep snow or mud, prevent standard postures. The Imam reinforces this by citing the Quranic verse to illustrate that human limitation is a valid basis for divine leniency.
